saad-ad-din-ii.s: Sa'ad ad-Din II was the last ruler of the Ifat Sultanate, a Muslim state of the Walashma dynasty in the Horn of Africa. He was captured and executed around 1410 during the campaigns of the Ethiopian Emperor Dawit I, forcing his surviving family into exile in Yemen.

saad-ibn-abi-waqqas.s: Saad ibn Abi Waqqas was an early companion of the Prophet Muhammad and a leading commander of the Rashidun Caliphate. He led the Arab army that defeated the Sasanian forces of Rostam Farrokhzad at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, opening Iraq to Muslim conquest.

saadi-dynasty.s: The Saadi dynasty was a family of Arab sharifs who ruled Morocco from the sixteenth to the mid-seventeenth century. Under Sultan Abd al-Malik its forces defeated a Portuguese invasion at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578, in which King Sebastian of Portugal was killed.

sabium.s: Sabium was an early king of the First Dynasty of Babylon in the nineteenth century BCE. He was one of the five rulers, from Sumuabum to Sin-muballit, who preceded Hammurabi.

sabr-ad-din-iii.s: Sabr ad-Din III was a prince of the Walashma dynasty who founded the Adal Sultanate in about 1415. He returned from exile in Yemen after the defeat of the Ifat Sultanate and the execution of its ruler, Sa'ad ad-Din II, by Ethiopian forces.

sabun.s: Sabun was a sultan of Wadai in the central Sahel who reigned from about 1803 to 1813. The Wadai Empire profile credits him with centralising administration, expanding the army and creating a more effective revenue collection system.

sack-of-angkor-1431.s: The sack of Angkor in 1431 was the capture of the Khmer capital by forces of the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya. It followed repeated invasions and came at a time when the Khmer Empire was already weakened by internal problems and shifting trade patterns.

sack-of-assur.s: The sack of Assur was the capture of the ancient Assyrian religious capital by the Medes in 614 BCE. It formed part of the joint campaign of the Medes and the Babylonians under Nabopolassar against the Assyrian Empire.

sack-of-constantinople-1204.s: The sack of Constantinople in 1204 was the capture and plunder of the Byzantine capital by the army of the Fourth Crusade, supported by Venice. The crusaders established a Latin Empire in the city, and the Byzantine state fragmented into successor states.

sack-of-delhi.s: The sack of Delhi in 1739 was the plundering of the Mughal capital by the army of Nader Shah, founder of the Afsharid Empire, after his victory at the Battle of Karnal. Nader carried off enormous wealth, including the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, and the Afsharid…

sack-of-delhi-1398.s: The sack of Delhi in 1398 was the capture and devastation of the capital of the Delhi Sultanate by the Central Asian conqueror Timur. Large numbers of inhabitants were killed, artisans were carried off to Samarkand and the treasury was emptied.

sack-of-koumbi-saleh.s: The sack of Koumbi Saleh refers to the capture of the capital of the Ghana Empire around 1076, traditionally attributed to the Almoravids. Koumbi Saleh was a double city made up of a royal town and a separate Muslim merchants' quarter.

sack-of-rome-410.s: The sack of Rome in 410 CE was the capture and plunder of the city by the Visigoths under Alaric. It was the first time in about eight centuries that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy, and it caused deep shock across the Roman world.

sack-of-surat.s: The sack of Surat in 1664 was a raid by the Maratha leader Shivaji on the wealthy Mughal port city of Surat in Gujarat. His forces seized large amounts of wealth from the city over several days.

sacred-kingship.s: Sacred kingship refers to the idea that a ruler possesses divine or supernatural qualities, or acts as an intermediary between the community and the spiritual world. In many African states it was a foundation of royal legitimacy and ritual.

sadr.s: Sadr was a title of high office in the Safavid state of Iran. In Safavid practice the sadr was closely associated with supervising the religious establishment and pious endowments, and the Safavid Empire profile also mentions the title alongside that of vakil in describing the…

safavid-empire.s: The Safavid Empire was a state that ruled Iran from 1501, when Ismail I proclaimed himself shah, until the fall of Isfahan to Afghan invaders in 1722. Founded on the Safaviyya Sufi order and its Qizilbash followers, it made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, shaping Iran's…

safaviyya.s: The Safaviyya was a Sufi religious order founded by Safi al-Din Ardabili in Ardabil in north-western Iran in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century. Over time it became increasingly militant and Shia in orientation and gained a devoted following among Turkmen tribes…

saffarid-dynasty.s: The Saffarid dynasty was a Persian dynasty founded in Sistan in eastern Iran in the ninth century by Yaqub ibn al-Layth, a former coppersmith. It conquered much of eastern Iran and challenged the authority of the Abbasid Caliphate, even marching towards Baghdad.

safi-al-din-ardabili.s: Safi al-Din Ardabili (1252–1334) was a Sufi master from Ardabil in north-western Iran and the founder of the Safaviyya order. His shrine in Ardabil became a major religious centre.

safi-of-persia.s: Safi of Persia, known as Shah Safi, was the Safavid ruler of Iran from 1629 to 1642 and the grandson of Shah Abbas I. His reign saw purges of officials and members of the royal family and the loss of Baghdad and Iraq to the Ottoman Empire.

sagres.s: Sagres is a town on the south-western tip of Portugal, overlooking the Atlantic. It is traditionally associated with Prince Henry the Navigator, who sponsored voyages of exploration along the West African coast from his base there.

sahara.s: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, covering most of northern Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. Trans-Saharan caravan routes carried gold, salt, slaves, textiles and ideas between North Africa and West Africa, sustaining empires on both sides of the desert.

sahel.s: The Sahel is the semi-arid belt of savannah and steppe stretching across Africa along the southern edge of the Sahara, from Senegal to Sudan. It formed a meeting zone between desert traders and the agricultural societies of the south, and its trading cities were linked to…

sahel-drought.s: The Sahel drought refers to a prolonged period of reduced rainfall in the Sahel during the twelfth century. According to the Ghana Empire profile, it damaged agricultural production in the region at a time when trade routes were already shifting away from Ghana.

sailendra-dynasty.s: The Sailendra dynasty was a ruling family in central Java in the eighth and ninth centuries, known for its patronage of Mahayana Buddhism. It is credited with building the great Buddhist monument of Borobudur.

saint-petersburg.s: Saint Petersburg is a city in north-western Russia on the Neva River, founded by Peter the Great in 1703 on territory conquered from Sweden. It was built as a purpose-built European capital and served as the capital of the Russian Empire for most of its history.

saint-domingue.s: Saint-Domingue was the French colony on the western part of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola. In the eighteenth century its sugar and coffee plantations, worked by enslaved Africans, made it one of the most profitable colonies in the world.

sajah.s: Sajah was a woman from the Tamim tribe of northern Arabia who claimed prophethood after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. She attracted a following and allied for a time with another claimant, Musaylima.

sakoku.s: Sakoku, often translated as closed country or maritime prohibition, was the foreign relations policy of the Tokugawa Shogunate, formalised in a series of edicts from 1633 to 1639. It banned most foreigners and Christianity, forbade Japanese from travelling abroad and limited…

saladin.s: Saladin (Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub) was a Kurdish Muslim military leader and the founder of the Ayyubid Empire, who died in 1193. He became vizier of Fatimid Egypt in 1169, ended the Fatimid Caliphate and united Egypt and Syria under his rule.

salammbo.s: Salammbô is a historical novel by the French writer Gustave Flaubert, published in 1862. It is set in Carthage during the Mercenary War of 241–238 BCE, when unpaid veterans of the First Punic War rebelled against the city.

salinisation.s: Salinisation is the build-up of salts in soil, often caused by long-term irrigation in hot, dry climates where evaporation leaves mineral deposits behind. It reduces crop yields and can make land unusable for farming.

salt-and-iron-monopoly.s: The salt and iron monopoly was a state monopoly over the production and sale of salt and iron established under Emperor Wu of the Han Dynasty in the second century BCE. It provided revenue for military campaigns against the Xiongnu and other state needs.

salt-trade.s: The salt trade refers to the long-distance exchange of salt, a vital commodity for human diet and food preservation. In West Africa, salt mined in the Sahara was carried south by caravan and traded for gold and other goods from the savannah and forest regions.

salvador.s: Salvador is a city on the north-eastern coast of Brazil, founded in 1549 by the first Governor-General, Tomé de Sousa. It served as the capital of Portuguese colonial Brazil until 1763 and was a major centre of the sugar economy and the Atlantic slave trade.

samanid-empire.s: The Samanid Empire was a Persian dynasty that ruled Khurasan and Transoxiana in the ninth and tenth centuries, initially as governors under the Abbasid Caliphate. Its capital Bukhara became a centre of the revival of Persian language and literature.

samarkand.s: Samarkand is an ancient city in modern Uzbekistan and one of the major centres of the Silk Road in Central Asia. It was captured by the Mongols, fell within the Chagatai Khanate and became the capital of the Timurid Empire, where Timur and his successors adorned it with…

samarra.s: Samarra is a city on the Tigris in Iraq, founded by the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim as a new capital in the ninth century. It housed the caliph's Turkic slave-soldier army away from Baghdad.

samori-ture.s: Samori Ture was a West African Muslim leader who built a large state, often called the Wassoulou Empire, in the late nineteenth century. He resisted French colonial expansion for many years before his capture in 1898.

samsu-iluna.s: Samsu-iluna was king of Babylon and the son and successor of Hammurabi. Shortly after his accession he faced a major rebellion of southern cities led by Rim-Sin II, which he crushed at the cost of destroying the walls of Ur, Uruk and Isin.

samudragupta.s: Samudragupta was an emperor of the Gupta Empire who reigned c. 335–375 CE.

samuel-de-champlain.s: Samuel de Champlain was a French explorer, navigator and colonial administrator who founded Quebec in 1608. He explored much of the St.

samurai.s: The samurai were the hereditary military class of pre-modern Japan. Under the Tokugawa Shogunate they became a largely administrative and bureaucratic elite in a long period of peace, paid fixed stipends in rice and expected to follow codes of loyalty and service.

sanaa.s: Sana'a is an ancient city in the highlands of Yemen and an important centre of South Arabia. In the sixth century the Aksumites installed a Christian ruler there after their invasion of Himyar.

sancai.s: Sancai, meaning three colours, is a type of Chinese lead-glazed pottery decorated mainly in amber, green and cream, which flourished under the Tang Dynasty. It was widely used for tomb figures, including horses and camels.

sanctions.s: Sanctions are penalties, usually economic, imposed by states or international bodies to pressure another state to change its behaviour. After Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, the League of Nations imposed sanctions on Italy.

sanjakbey.s: A sanjakbey (sancakbey) was the governor of a sanjak, a district-level province of the Ottoman Empire. Sanjakbeys held military and administrative authority, commanded the local timariot cavalry and answered to the beylerbeys who governed larger provinces.

sankin-kotai.s: Sankin-kōtai, or alternate attendance, was a system of the Tokugawa Shogunate requiring daimyo to divide their time between their domains and the shogun's capital at Edo, leaving their families in Edo as hostages. The costly journeys and households drained the lords' resources…

sankore-madrasah.s: The Sankore Madrasah was an Islamic centre of learning based around the Sankore Mosque in Timbuktu. Together with other mosques and scholarly households in the city it formed a renowned network of teaching in theology, law, astronomy and other subjects.

sanskrit.s: Sanskrit is a classical Indo-Aryan language of South Asia, used for religious, literary, philosophical and scientific texts over more than three millennia. Under the Gupta Empire classical Sanskrit literature reached its peak, with poets such as Kalidasa.

santeria.s: Santería is an Afro-Cuban religion that developed among enslaved Yoruba people and their descendants in Cuba, blending Yoruba spiritual traditions with elements of Roman Catholicism. It centres on the worship of deities known as orishas.

sao-paulo.s: São Paulo is a region of south-eastern Brazil, now a state, centred on the city of the same name. In the nineteenth century it became the heart of Brazil's booming coffee economy.

sao-tome.s: São Tomé is an island in the Gulf of Guinea off the coast of Central Africa, settled by the Portuguese in the late fifteenth century. It became an early centre of plantation sugar production using enslaved African labour and a hub of the slave trade.

saqifah.s: Saqifah refers to the meeting held in 632 CE at the Saqifah, a covered gathering place of the Banu Sa'ida in Medina, where companions of the Prophet Muhammad debated the succession within hours of his death. The gathering resulted in the selection of Abu Bakr as the first caliph.

sarajevo.s: Sarajevo is the principal city of Bosnia, which came under Austro-Hungarian administration in 1878 and was annexed in 1908. On 28 June 1914 the heir to the Habsburg throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, was assassinated there by the Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip.

sardar.s: Sardar is a Persian-derived title meaning chief or commander, used in South Asia for nobles, military leaders and heads of armed bands. In the Maratha Empire, sardars were noble chieftains who commanded troops, governed provinces and enjoyed considerable autonomy.

sardeshmukhi.s: Sardeshmukhi was an additional levy, traditionally reckoned at a tenth of revenue, claimed by the Maratha rulers on top of the chauth. It was justified as the due of a hereditary overlord and was collected from territories under Maratha influence.

sardinia.s: Sardinia is a large island in the western Mediterranean, west of the Italian peninsula. Carthage established control over much of it, using it as a source of grain, metals and soldiers.

sardis.s: Sardis was the capital of the kingdom of Lydia in western Anatolia. Cyrus the Great captured it in 546 BCE after defeating King Croesus, and it became a major Achaemenid administrative centre.

sargon-ii.s: Sargon II was a king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire in the late eighth century BCE, who founded a new capital at Dur-Sharrukin. His reign saw extensive campaigns across the Near East.

sargon-of-akkad.s: Sargon of Akkad was the founder of the Akkadian Empire, whose reign is conventionally dated from c. 2334 BCE.

sarissa.s: The sarissa was a very long pike, several metres in length, carried by the infantry of the Macedonian phalanx. Introduced under Philip II, it allowed several ranks of soldiers to present their points to the enemy at once.

sarkel.s: Sarkel was a fortress and town on the lower Don River, built for the Khazars in the ninth century with Byzantine assistance. It served as a defensive stronghold and a centre of trade and administration.

sarsa-dengel.s: Sarsa Dengel was Emperor of Ethiopia in the second half of the sixteenth century. According to the Adal Sultanate profile, he defeated and executed the Adal Sultan Muhammad V in 1577.

sasan.s: Sasan was a figure from whom the Sasanian dynasty of Iran took its name. Tradition describes him as a Zoroastrian priest and ancestor of Ardashir I, the founder of the Sasanian Empire.

sasanian-conquest-of-jerusalem.s: The Sasanian conquest of Jerusalem took place in 614 CE, when the city fell to the forces of Khosrow II under his general Shahrbaraz during the last great war between the Sasanian and Byzantine empires. The relic of the True Cross was carried off to Persia.

sasanian-conquest-of-yemen.s: The Sasanian conquest of Yemen was the campaign of c. 570–578 CE in which a Persian expeditionary force expelled the Aksumite-backed regime from South Arabia.

sasanian-empire.s: The Sasanian Empire was the last pre-Islamic Persian empire, founded by Ardashir I in the third century CE after overthrowing the Parthian Empire. Centred on Ctesiphon, it was a great rival of Rome and Byzantium, with Zoroastrianism as its state religion.

satrapy.s: A satrapy was a province of the Achaemenid Empire governed by a satrap, a royal governor responsible for taxation, security and administration. Darius I organised the empire into satrapies assessed for fixed tribute.

satsuma-domain.s: The Satsuma Domain was a powerful feudal domain in southern Kyushu, ruled by the Shimazu family. During the late Tokugawa period it acquired Western weapons and military training.

savannah.s: Savannah is a type of tropical grassland with scattered trees, found widely across Africa between the rainforest and the desert. Its open terrain favoured cavalry warfare, cattle herding and grain farming.

savaran.s: The savaran were the heavy cavalry of the Sasanian Empire, with horse and rider protected by armour. Drawn largely from the aristocracy, they formed the elite striking force of the Sasanian army.

sawad.s: The Sawad was the name given by Arab writers to the fertile, irrigated lowlands of southern and central Iraq between the Tigris and Euphrates. Its dense agriculture made it one of the richest regions of the Islamic world.

saxon-wars.s: The Saxon Wars were the campaigns fought from 772 to 804 by Charlemagne against the Saxons, a Germanic people living east of the Rhine. The conflict involved repeated annual campaigns, mass deportations and the forced Christianisation of the Saxons.

saxons.s: The Saxons were a Germanic people of northern Germany, whose name was later carried by the duchy and electorate of Saxony. Charlemagne conquered them in the Saxon Wars, and their region later produced the Ottonian dynasty of the Holy Roman Empire.

saxons-people.s: Saxons here refers to the inhabitants and forces of the Electorate of Saxony in early modern Germany. Saxony was involved in the wars of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, including the Great Northern War, in which its elector Augustus II, also King of Poland,…

sayf-ibn-dhi-yazan.s: Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan was a semi-legendary Himyarite king of Yemen, remembered in Arabic folk tradition. The Sayfawa dynasty of Kanem claimed descent from him, and the dynasty took its name from his.

sayfawa-dynasty.s: The Sayfawa dynasty was the ruling house of Kanem and later Bornu around Lake Chad, which claimed descent from Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan. It ruled for many centuries, making it one of the longest-lasting dynasties in African history, until it was displaced in the nineteenth century.

sayyid-dynasty.s: The Sayyid dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate in the first half of the fifteenth century, after Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398. Its founder, Khizr Khan, had served as a Timurid governor.

scandinavia.s: Scandinavia is the region of northern Europe comprising Denmark, Norway and Sweden. In the Viking Age Scandinavian traders used river routes such as the Volga, through which silver dirhams flowed northward via Khazar territory, as the Khazar Khaganate profile notes.

scania.s: Scania is the southernmost province of modern Sweden, facing Denmark across the Øresund strait. Long part of Denmark, it was ceded to Sweden by the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658.

schlieffen-plan.s: The Schlieffen Plan was the German military plan, named after the chief of the general staff Alfred von Schlieffen, for fighting a two-front war against France and Russia. It envisaged a rapid sweep through Belgium to defeat France before turning east.

scholar-officials.s: Scholar-officials were the educated class of imperial China who staffed the civil service after passing the state examinations based on the Confucian classics. They combined literary learning with administrative responsibility and enjoyed high social prestige.

scholasticism.s: Scholasticism was the dominant method of philosophy and theology in the universities of medieval Europe, which sought to reconcile Christian doctrine with reason, especially the philosophy of Aristotle. The Almohad Caliphate profile notes that the commentaries on Aristotle by…

scientific-revolution.s: The Scientific Revolution was the period, roughly the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, in which new methods of observation, experiment and mathematics transformed European understanding of nature. Figures such as Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo and Newton are associated with it.

scindias.s: The Scindias were a Maratha ruling family who became one of the most powerful houses of the Maratha Confederacy, later based at Gwalior. Along with the Holkars, Gaekwads and Bhonsles, they held large territories in northern and central India.

scipio-aemilianus.s: Scipio Aemilianus was a Roman general and statesman who commanded the final siege of Carthage during the Third Punic War. In 146 BCE he captured and destroyed the city.

scipio-family.s: The Scipio family was a leading branch of the Roman Cornelii, prominent in the Roman Republic. During the Second Punic War its members fought Carthaginian forces in Spain, and Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE.

scopas.s: Scopas was an Aetolian mercenary general who commanded the Ptolemaic army during the Fifth Syrian War. He was defeated by the Seleucid king Antiochus III at the Battle of Panium.

scotland.s: Scotland is a country occupying the northern part of Great Britain. Roman forces campaigned there but never fully conquered it, as the Roman Empire profile notes.

scramble-for-africa.s: The Scramble for Africa was the rapid partition and colonisation of most of the African continent by European powers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It was given diplomatic form by the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885.

scythian-interregnum.s: The Scythian Interregnum refers to the period c. 653–625 BCE when, according to ancient tradition, Scythian nomads dominated the Medes and imposed vassalage on Media.

scythians.s: The Scythians were a group of Iranian-speaking nomadic peoples who dominated the Eurasian steppe north of the Black Sea and beyond in the first millennium BCE. Renowned as mounted archers, they interacted with and raided the settled empires of the Near East.

sea-of-galilee.s: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake in the northern Levant, fed by the Jordan River. In 1187 Saladin's forces manoeuvred the Crusader army into waterless terrain nearby and denied it access to the lake.

sea-peoples.s: The Sea Peoples were migrating confederacies of seafaring raiders who attacked the eastern Mediterranean at the end of the Late Bronze Age. Egyptian records describe Ramesses III defeating them in land and sea battles around c.

sealand-dynasty.s: The Sealand Dynasty was a line of rulers in the marshy far south of Mesopotamia that broke away from Babylon after the death of Hammurabi. According to the Babylonian Empire profile, it was founded by Ilum-ma-ili after defeating Samsu-iluna.

sebastian-of-portugal.s: Sebastian of Portugal (Sebastião I) was King of Portugal from 1557 until 1578. He led an invasion of Morocco that ended in disaster at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578, where he was killed and his army destroyed by Saadi forces.

second-anglo-sikh-war.s: The Second Anglo-Sikh War was fought in 1848–1849 between the Sikh Empire and the British East India Company. It was triggered by uprisings at Multan and Hazara.

second-arab-siege-of-constantinople.s: The Second Arab siege of Constantinople was a land and sea assault on the Byzantine capital by the Umayyad Caliphate in 717–718 CE. The defenders under Emperor Leo III, helped by Greek fire, a harsh winter and Bulgar attacks, forced the Arab army to withdraw with heavy losses.

second-battle-of-el-alamein.s: The Second Battle of El Alamein was fought in Egypt in 1942 between British Commonwealth forces under Bernard Montgomery and the German-Italian army under Erwin Rommel. The Allied victory forced the Axis armies into a long retreat across North Africa.

second-boer-war.s: The Second Boer War was fought from 1899 to 1902 between the British Empire and the two Boer republics, the South African Republic and the Orange Free State. After early setbacks, Britain deployed large forces, used scorched-earth tactics and interned civilians in…

second-fitna.s: The Second Fitna was a period of civil war in the Islamic caliphate from 680 to 692. It began after the accession of Yazid I and included the death of Husayn ibn Ali at Karbala and the rival caliphate of Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca.

second-intermediate-period.s: The Second Intermediate Period was the era of political fragmentation in ancient Egypt between the Middle Kingdom and the New Kingdom, when the Hyksos ruled the north. The Egyptian Empire New Kingdom profile describes how rulers from Thebes expelled the Hyksos and reunified…

second-italian-war-of-independence.s: The Second Italian War of Independence was fought in 1859 by France and the Kingdom of Sardinia against the Austrian Empire. Austrian defeats at Magenta and Solferino led to the loss of Lombardy.

second-italo-ethiopian-war.s: The Second Italo-Ethiopian War was Fascist Italy's invasion and conquest of Ethiopia in 1935–1936. Italian forces used aircraft and poison gas, and Emperor Haile Selassie went into exile.

second-luba-dynasty.s: The Second Luba Dynasty was the ruling line of the Luba Empire established by Kalala Ilunga around 1585, after he defeated and executed the earlier ruler Nkongolo. It introduced a sacred kingship system known as the balopwe.

second-partition-of-poland.s: The Second Partition of Poland was the annexation of large parts of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth by Russia and Prussia in 1793. It followed the Constitution of 3 May 1791 and Russian intervention against the reformers.

second-persian-invasion-of-greece.s: The Second Persian invasion of Greece was the massive campaign launched by Xerxes I of the Achaemenid Empire in 480 BCE. It included the Persian victory at Thermopylae and the sack of Athens, but Greek victories at Salamis and later Plataea forced the Persians to withdraw.

second-punic-war.s: The Second Punic War was fought from 218 to 201 BCE between Carthage and Rome. Hannibal invaded Italy across the Alps and won great victories such as Cannae, but could not force Rome to surrender, while Roman forces conquered Carthaginian Spain.

second-serfdom.s: The second serfdom refers to the tightening of serfdom in central and eastern Europe from the late fifteenth century onwards, at a time when serfdom was declining in western Europe. It was linked to the growth of grain exports to western markets.

second-triumvirate.s: The Second Triumvirate was the political alliance formed in 43 BCE by Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus to rule the Roman state after the assassination of Julius Caesar. It defeated Caesar's assassins and carried out proscriptions of its opponents.

second-turkic-khaganate.s: The Second Turkic Khaganate was the revived Göktürk state established in the late seventh century, after a period of subjection to Tang China. It is known for the Orkhon inscriptions, the earliest substantial texts in a Turkic language.

second-viennese-school.s: The Second Viennese School was a group of composers centred on Arnold Schoenberg and his pupils Alban Berg and Anton Webern in early twentieth-century Vienna. They developed atonality and later the twelve-tone method, transforming Western classical music.

second-world-war.s: The Second World War was the global conflict of 1939 to 1945 between the Allies and the Axis powers, the deadliest war in history. It destroyed the Italian Empire, whose African colonies were lost to Allied forces, and fatally weakened the British Empire, accelerating…

secret-society.s: A secret society is an organisation whose membership, rituals or knowledge are restricted to initiates. In the Luba Empire the Bambudye society acted as custodian of historical memory and as a check on royal excess.

secretariat-chancellery.s: The Secretariat-Chancellery was the chief administrative organ of the central government of the Song Dynasty. It worked alongside the Bureau of Military Affairs and the Finance Commission.

sejm.s: The Sejm was the parliament of the Kingdom of Poland and later of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, made up of the king, the senate and representatives of the nobility. It held wide powers over taxation, legislation and the election of kings.

seku-amadu.s: Seku Amadu (Ahmadu Lobbo) was a Fulani Muslim scholar and reformer who launched a jihad in Massina in the inner Niger delta in 1818 and founded the state known as the Massina Caliphate. The Sokoto Caliphate profile lists his movement among the West African jihads that were…

seleucia.s: Seleucia, or Seleucia-on-Tigris, was a city founded by Seleucus I Nicator in Mesopotamia around the end of the fourth century BCE. It served as one of the twin capitals of the Seleucid Empire alongside Antioch and became one of the largest cities of the Hellenistic world.

seleucid-empire.s: The Seleucid Empire was a Hellenistic state founded by Seleucus I Nicator, one of Alexander the Great's generals, after the break-up of the Macedonian Empire. At its height it stretched from Anatolia and Syria to Central Asia, ruling from Antioch and Seleucia.

seleucid-era.s: The Seleucid era was a system of dating years from the recovery of Babylon by Seleucus I Nicator in 312/311 BCE. According to the Seleucid Empire profile, Seleucus adopted this event as the foundation date of his empire.

seleucid-mauryan-war.s: The Seleucid–Mauryan war was the conflict between Seleucus I Nicator and Chandragupta Maurya at the end of the fourth century BCE, which ended in a peace settlement often called the Treaty of the Indus. Seleucus ceded territories in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent…

seleucus-i-nicator.s: Seleucus I Nicator was a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great and the founder of the Seleucid Empire. After Alexander's death he secured Babylon and built a realm stretching from Anatolia to the borders of India.

self-determination.s: Self-determination is the principle that peoples have the right to choose their own political status and form of government. Promoted by Woodrow Wilson at the end of the First World War, it guided the redrawing of borders in central and eastern Europe.

self-strengthening-movement.s: The Self-Strengthening Movement was a programme of reform in the Qing Empire from the 1860s to the 1880s, which aimed to adopt Western military technology and industry while preserving the Confucian order. It produced arsenals, shipyards and modern enterprises.

selim-i.s: Selim I was Ottoman sultan from 1512 to 1520. He defeated the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514 and conquered the Mamluk Sultanate in 1516–1517, bringing Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia under Ottoman rule.

selimiye-mosque.s: The Selimiye Mosque is an imperial mosque in Edirne built for Sultan Selim II by the architect Mimar Sinan in the 1570s. Its vast central dome and four slender minarets make it one of the masterpieces of Ottoman architecture.

seljuk-warlord.s: Seljuk, or Seljuk Beg, was a chieftain of the Qiniq clan of the Oghuz Turks, from whom the Seljuk dynasty took its name. According to the Seljuk Empire profile, around 985 CE he converted to Sunni Islam and moved with his followers towards the frontiers of the Islamic world.

seljuk-empire.s: The Seljuk Empire, or Great Seljuk Empire, was a Sunni Turkic state founded in the eleventh century by descendants of Seljuk Beg. It conquered Iran, took control of Baghdad from the Buyids and defeated the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

semirechye.s: Semirechye, meaning seven rivers, is a region of steppe and river valleys south-east of Lake Balkhash, in modern Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. It was valued as pastureland by nomadic peoples.

semitic-languages.s: The Semitic languages are a family of languages of the Near East and North Africa that includes Akkadian, Aramaic, Hebrew, Phoenician, Arabic and Ge'ez. Akkadian was the first Semitic language to be widely written, and the Akkadian Empire profile notes its role in…

semu.s: Semu was a category in the social hierarchy of the Yuan Dynasty, covering peoples of Central and Western Asian origin. Ranked below the Mongols but above northern and southern Chinese, the Semu held many administrative and financial posts.

senegal.s: Senegal is a region of westernmost Africa, named after the Senegal River and now an independent country. It was home to states such as the Jolof Empire and was a frontier of the Almoravid movement and the Mali Empire.

senegal-river.s: The Senegal River flows from the Guinea highlands to the Atlantic, forming much of the border between modern Senegal and Mauritania. Its valley was an important agricultural and trading zone at the southern edge of the Sahara.

senegambia.s: Senegambia is the region of West Africa between the Senegal and Gambia rivers. It was dominated for a time by the Jolof Empire and was later home to the Kaabu Empire.

sengoku-period.s: The Sengoku period, or Warring States period, was an era of almost continuous civil war in Japan from the late fifteenth to the late sixteenth century. Regional lords fought for power while central authority collapsed.

sennacherib.s: Sennacherib was king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BCE, known for rebuilding Nineveh as a magnificent capital. He fought repeated wars against Babylon and Elam and destroyed Babylon in 689 BCE.

sennacheribs-destruction-of-babylon.s: Sennacherib's destruction of Babylon took place in 689 BCE, when the Assyrian king captured the city after repeated rebellions and had it devastated. The act shocked the Mesopotamian world because of Babylon's religious prestige.

senussi-order.s: The Senussi order (Sanusiyya) was a Sufi religious and political brotherhood founded in the nineteenth century and centred in Cyrenaica in Libya. It organised resistance to French and Italian colonial expansion in the Sahara.

septimius-severus.s: Septimius Severus was Roman emperor from 193 to 211 CE, born in Leptis Magna in North Africa. The Garamantian Empire profile notes that he mounted a campaign against the Garamantes in 202 CE.

serbia.s: Serbia is a country in the central Balkans, home to the Serbs, whose medieval kingdom was strongly influenced by the Byzantine Empire. In the nineteenth century it regained independence from the Ottomans and became a rival of Austria-Hungary.

serbs.s: The Serbs are a South Slavic people of the Balkans, predominantly Orthodox Christian. Large Serb communities lived within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, especially in Croatia, Vojvodina and Bosnia.

serer.s: The Serer are a people of the Senegambia region of West Africa, known for their distinct religious traditions and kingdoms such as Sine and Saloum. The Jolof Empire profile mentions the Serer among the neighbouring peoples and states whose interactions shaped the regional…

serfdom.s: Serfdom was a form of unfree labour in which peasants were bound to the land and owed labour or dues to a lord. It was widespread in medieval Europe and lasted longest in central and eastern Europe.

sergei-witte.s: Sergei Witte was a Russian statesman who served as minister of finance in the 1890s and early 1900s and later as prime minister. He promoted rapid industrialisation, the Trans-Siberian Railway and the gold standard.

sericulture.s: Sericulture is the raising of silkworms for the production of raw silk, typically by feeding them on mulberry leaves. It originated in China and was long a closely guarded skill.

sesame.s: Sesame is a flowering plant cultivated for its oil-rich seeds, one of the oldest oilseed crops. It was grown widely in ancient Mesopotamia and the Near East.

seven-years-war.s: The Seven Years' War was a global conflict fought from 1756 to 1763 between Britain, Prussia and their allies and France, Austria, Russia and their allies. Fighting took place in Europe, North America, India and the Caribbean.

seventy-seven-laws.s: The Seventy-Seven Laws were a code of laws traditionally attributed to Okomfo Anokye, the priest associated with the founding of the Ashanti Empire. The Ashanti Empire profile describes them as a codified constitution for the new state.

seville.s: Seville is a city in Andalusia in southern Spain, on the Guadalquivir River. It served as a capital of the Almohad Caliphate in al-Andalus, where the Almohads built the great mosque whose minaret survives as the Giralda.

sexagenarian-law.s: The Sexagenarian Law was a Brazilian law passed in 1885 that freed enslaved people aged sixty and over. It was one of the gradual abolition measures, following the Law of the Free Womb of 1871 and preceding the Lei Áurea of 1888.

seychelles.s: The Seychelles is an archipelago in the western Indian Ocean, which was a British colony from the early nineteenth century. The British used it as a place of exile for deposed rulers.

shafii-school.s: The Shafi'i school is one of the four major schools of Sunni Islamic law, named after the jurist al-Shafi'i. It became widespread in Egypt, Syria and parts of Iran and South-East Asia.

shah-title.s: Shah is a Persian royal title meaning king, used by rulers of Iran from ancient times. It was the title of the Sasanian monarchs and later of the Khwarazmian, Safavid, Afsharid and Zand rulers.

shah-mosque.s: The Shah Mosque, also known as the Imam Mosque, is a great congregational mosque on the Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan, built under Shah Abbas I in the early seventeenth century. It is famous for its tile decoration and monumental domes.

shah-rukh.s: Shah Rukh was a son of Timur who ruled the Timurid Empire from 1409 to 1447, governing from Herat. His reign brought relative stability and a flourishing of Persian art and literature.

shahanshah.s: Shahanshah, meaning King of Kings, was the title of the supreme ruler in ancient and medieval Iran. It was used by the Achaemenid kings and revived by the Sasanian dynasty, whose founder Ardashir I adopted it.

shahr-province.s: A shahr was a province of the Sasanian Empire. According to the Sasanian Empire profile, these provinces were governed by marzbans, who were responsible for both civil administration and frontier defence.

shahrbaraz.s: Shahrbaraz was a leading Sasanian general under Khosrow II. He captured Jerusalem from the Byzantines in 614 CE and led campaigns deep into Byzantine territory.

shahrokh-shah.s: Shahrokh Shah was a grandson of Nader Shah who reigned as a nominal Afsharid ruler in Mashhad after being blinded. The Afsharid Empire profile notes that he survived until 1796, when Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar took the city and had him tortured to death.

shajar-al-durr.s: Shajar al-Durr was the widow of the Ayyubid sultan al-Salih Ayyub, who ruled Egypt as sultan in 1250. Her brief rule marked the transition from Ayyubid to Mamluk power.

shaka-zulu-king.s: Shaka was the king of the Zulu who built the Zulu kingdom into a powerful military state in south-eastern Africa from the 1810s. His wars and state-building are associated with the Mfecane, a period of upheaval and migration across southern Africa.

shalmaneser-i.s: Shalmaneser I was a king of Assyria in the thirteenth century BCE. The Mitanni Empire profile notes that he suppressed rebellions in the Mitanni rump state, also called Hanigalbat.

shamanism.s: Shamanism refers to religious practices centred on a shaman, a figure believed to communicate with spirits through trance and ritual. It was widespread among the peoples of the Eurasian steppe, including the Mongols.

shamshi-adad-i.s: Shamshi-Adad I was an Amorite ruler who reigned c. 1808–1776 BCE and built a kingdom across northern Mesopotamia, including the city of Assur.

shanhai-pass.s: The Shanhai Pass is a strategic pass at the eastern end of the Great Wall, between the mountains and the sea. In 1644 the Ming general Wu Sangui opened it to Manchu forces to fight the rebel Li Zicheng, who had seized Beijing.

shanxi.s: Shanxi is a province of northern China, rich in coal and iron. The Song Dynasty profile notes that coal and iron production in Hebei and Shanxi reached a scale not surpassed in Europe until the eighteenth century.

shapur-i.s: Shapur I was the second king of the Sasanian Empire, who reigned from 241 to 272 CE. He defeated several Roman emperors, capturing Antioch and taking Emperor Valerian prisoner at Edessa in 260 CE.

shapur-ii.s: Shapur II was a king of the Sasanian Empire who reigned for most of the fourth century CE. He fought long wars against Rome, capturing Amida in 359 CE.

sharia.s: Sharia refers to Islamic law, the body of religious and legal rules derived from the Quran, the example of the Prophet and the work of jurists. It governed matters of worship, family, contract and crime.

shar-kali-sharri.s: Shar-Kali-Sharri was the last powerful king of the Akkadian Empire and a son of Naram-Sin. His reign saw growing pressure from the Gutians and other enemies and internal revolts.

shattiwaza.s: Shattiwaza was a king of Mitanni in the fourteenth century BCE. After the assassination of his father Tushratta and a disputed succession, he turned to the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I.

shattiwaza-treaty.s: The Shattiwaza treaty was a treaty concluded c. 1330 BCE between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza of Mitanni.

shattuara-i.s: Shattuara I was a ruler of the Mitanni rump state of Hanigalbat in the thirteenth century BCE. According to the Mitanni Empire profile, he led a rebellion against Assyrian domination that was suppressed.

shaushtatar.s: Shaushtatar was a king of Mitanni around c. 1450 BCE, under whom the kingdom reached a peak of power.

shawl.s: A shawl is a large piece of cloth worn over the shoulders or head. Kashmir was famous for fine shawls woven from pashmina wool, which became luxury goods sought in Europe.

shaybanids.s: The Shaybanids were an Uzbek dynasty descended from Shiban, a grandson of Genghis Khan, who ruled much of Central Asia in the sixteenth century. Under Muhammad Shaybani Khan they captured Samarkand, Bukhara and Herat between 1500 and 1507.

sheikh-lotfollah-mosque.s: The Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque is a mosque on the eastern side of the Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan, built under Shah Abbas I in the early seventeenth century. It is renowned for the tilework of its dome and interior.

sheikh-ul-islam.s: Sheikh ul-Islam was the title of the chief religious authority in the Ottoman Empire, who headed the learned hierarchy of Islamic scholars. The holder issued legal opinions (fatwas) on matters of law and state policy.

sher-singh.s: Sher Singh was a son of Maharaja Ranjit Singh who ruled the Sikh Empire for a short period after the deaths of his predecessors. He was assassinated in 1843 amid factional struggles at the Lahore court.

shia-islam.s: Shia Islam is one of the two main branches of Islam, whose adherents hold that leadership of the community belonged to Ali ibn Abi Talib and his descendants. It emerged from the succession disputes described in the Rashidun Caliphate and Umayyad Caliphate profiles.

shia-islam-idea.s: Shi'a Islam is the branch of Islam that recognises Ali ibn Abi Talib and his descendants as the rightful leaders of the Muslim community. The Abbasid Caliphate drew on support from pro-Alid groups in its revolution against the Umayyads.

shifting-trade-routes.s: Shifting trade routes refers to the recurring pattern in which empires that depended on controlling commerce declined when trade moved to new routes. Changes in caravan paths, the rise of maritime routes or new competitors could cut revenues that sustained armies and…

shiism.s: Shi'ism is the branch of Islam that holds that leadership of the community belongs to the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib. Its Ismaili form was the faith of the Fatimid Caliphate, whose decline ended Ismaili rule in Egypt.

shilhak-inshushinak.s: Shilhak-Inshushinak was a king of Elam in the twelfth century BCE of the Shutrukid dynasty. Under him, according to the Elamite Confederation profile, Elamite territory extended from Mesopotamia east of the Tigris nearly to Persepolis.

shimashki-dynasty.s: The Shimashki dynasty was a line of rulers from the Iranian highlands who dominated Elam around the end of the third millennium BCE. Its king Kindattu captured Ur around 2004 BCE and took the last ruler of the Third Dynasty of Ur captive.

shiraz.s: Shiraz is a city in south-western Iran, known for its gardens and poets such as Hafez and Saadi. Karim Khan Zand made it the capital of the Zand Empire and adorned it with mosques, bazaars and a citadel.

shirkuh.s: Shirkuh was a Kurdish general in the service of the Zengid ruler Nur al-Din, and the uncle of Saladin. He led expeditions to Egypt and became vizier of the Fatimid Caliphate, dying in 1169.

shivaji.s: Shivaji (1630–1680) was the founder of the Maratha state in western India and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. He fought the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire using hill forts, guerrilla tactics and a navy.

shogun.s: Shōgun was the title of the military rulers of Japan, short for Seii Taishōgun, meaning barbarian-subduing generalissimo. Shoguns held real power while the emperor retained ceremonial authority.

shona.s: The Shona are a Bantu-speaking people of the Zimbabwean plateau and neighbouring areas. They formed the population of states such as Great Zimbabwe, the Mutapa Empire and the Rozvi Empire.

shulgi.s: Shulgi was the second king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, reigning c. 2094–2047 BCE.

shunga-empire.s: The Shunga Empire was a dynasty that ruled parts of northern and central India from the second century BCE. It was founded by Pushyamitra Shunga, a general who overthrew the last Mauryan ruler.

shunzhi-emperor.s: The Shunzhi Emperor was the first emperor of the Qing Dynasty to rule over China, enthroned in Beijing in 1644 while still a child. During his reign, regents and generals continued campaigns against Ming loyalists in the south.

shushtar.s: Shushtar is a city in south-western Iran on the Karun River. The Sasanian Empire profile notes that the Band-e Kaisar dam was built across the river near Shushtar using Roman engineering expertise from prisoners captured in Shapur I's campaigns.

shutrukid-dynasty.s: The Shutrukid dynasty was a ruling line of Elam in the twelfth century BCE under which Elam reached its military zenith. Its kings Shutruk-Nahhunte and Kutir-Nahhunte defeated the Kassite dynasty of Babylon.

shutruk-nahhunte.s: Shutruk-Nahhunte was a king of Elam of the Shutrukid dynasty in the twelfth century BCE. Together with his son Kutir-Nahhunte he defeated the Kassite dynasty of Babylon around 1158 BCE.

siberia.s: Siberia is the vast region of northern Asia extending from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific. Russian expansion across it began in the late sixteenth century, driven by the fur trade, and continued into the nineteenth century.

sichuan.s: Sichuan is a province of south-western China, centred on a fertile basin. Under the Song Dynasty it was an important economic region where early paper money developed.

sicily.s: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean, off the southern tip of Italy. Carthage and the Greek cities fought over it for centuries, and its loss to Rome after the First Punic War was a major blow to the Punic Empire.

siddis.s: The Siddis are a community of African descent in South Asia. On the western coast of India, Siddi rulers of Janjira maintained a naval power.

siege-capability.s: Siege capability refers to the recurring pattern in which an empire's ability to capture fortified cities determined how far it could expand. Siege engines, sapping, blockade and later artillery allowed armies to take strongholds that would otherwise resist.

siege-engine.s: A siege engine is a device designed to break or bypass fortifications, such as a battering ram, siege tower, catapult or trebuchet. The Mongol Empire used engineers from China and the Islamic world to build and operate siege engines.

siege-of-acre-1189-1191.s: The Siege of Acre (1189–1191) was a long siege of the port city of Acre during the Third Crusade. Crusader forces, later joined by Richard I of England and Philip II of France, eventually captured the city from Saladin's garrison.

siege-of-alamut.s: The Siege of Alamut was the capture of the mountain fortress of the Nizari Ismailis in northern Iran by Mongol forces under Hulagu in 1256. It ended the Nizari Ismaili state.

siege-of-amida-359.s: The Siege of Amida in 359 CE was the capture of the Roman city of Amida, modern Diyarbakir, by the Sasanian king Shapur II. According to the Sasanian Empire profile, the city fell after a 73-day siege.

siege-of-antioch-256.s: The Siege of Antioch in 256 CE was the capture of the great Roman city of Antioch by the Sasanian king Shapur I. The Sasanian Empire profile cites it as an example of Sasanian siege capability.

siege-of-baghdad-1258.s: The Siege of Baghdad in 1258 was the capture and sack of the Abbasid capital by the Mongol army of Hulagu. The caliph al-Musta'sim was executed and much of the city's population killed.

siege-of-basra-1775-1776.s: The Siege of Basra (1775–1776) was the capture of the Ottoman-held port city of Basra by the forces of the Zand Empire under Karim Khan. The Zand Empire profile notes that the Zands expelled the Ottomans from Basra in 1776.

siege-of-belgrade-1521.s: The Siege of Belgrade in 1521 was the capture of the Hungarian fortress city by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. It opened the way for the invasion of Hungary, which culminated at the Battle of Mohács in 1526.

siege-of-bursa.s: The Siege of Bursa was the long Ottoman blockade of the Byzantine city of Bursa in north-western Anatolia, which surrendered in 1326 to Orhan, son of Osman I. Bursa became the first major Ottoman capital.

siege-of-carthage-149-146-bce.s: The Siege of Carthage was the main engagement of the Third Punic War, in which Roman forces besieged the city of Carthage. In 146 BCE Scipio Aemilianus took the city, which was systematically demolished and its population killed or enslaved.

siege-of-djenne.s: The Siege of Djenné was a long siege of the trading city of Djenné in the inner Niger delta by the Songhai ruler Sunni Ali. According to the Songhai Empire profile, the city resisted for seven years before surrendering around c.

siege-of-fredriksten.s: The Siege of Fredriksten was the siege of a Norwegian fortress by Swedish forces in 1718, during King Charles XII's invasion of Norway. Charles was killed by a bullet in the siege trenches.

siege-of-isfahan.s: The Siege of Isfahan was the siege of the Safavid capital by Afghan forces under Mahmud Hotaki in 1722. After months of famine, Shah Sultan Husayn surrendered and abdicated.

siege-of-jerusalem-1099.s: The Siege of Jerusalem in 1099 was the capture of Jerusalem by the armies of the First Crusade, followed by a massacre of many of its inhabitants. It led to the creation of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem.

siege-of-jerusalem-1187.s: The Siege of Jerusalem in 1187 was the recapture of Jerusalem by Saladin after his victory over the Crusaders at Hattin. The city surrendered on terms that allowed many inhabitants to ransom themselves.

siege-of-jerusalem-587-bce.s: The Siege of Jerusalem in 587 BCE was the capture and destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldean (Neo-Babylonian) king Nebuchadnezzar II. The Temple was destroyed and much of the population was deported to Babylon.

siege-of-jerusalem-597-bce.s: The Siege of Jerusalem in 597 BCE was the capture of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire after the kingdom of Judah rebelled. King Jehoiachin and many leading citizens were deported to Babylon.

siege-of-kerman.s: The Siege of Kerman was the final siege in 1794 in which the Qajar leader Agha Mohammad Khan captured the city of Kerman from Lotf Ali Khan, the last Zand ruler. The Zand Empire profile notes that the city's inhabitants were punished by mass blinding.

siege-of-multan-1818.s: The Siege of Multan in 1818 was the capture of the city of Multan from its Afghan governor by the forces of Ranjit Singh. The Sikh Empire profile cites it as one of the conquests that extended Sikh rule.

siege-of-osaka.s: The Siege of Osaka was a series of campaigns in 1614–1615 in which the forces of Tokugawa Ieyasu attacked Osaka Castle, held by the Toyotomi family. The castle fell and the Toyotomi line was destroyed.

siege-of-paris-885-886.s: The Siege of Paris (885–886) was a siege of Paris by a large Viking army. The city was defended by Count Odo, while Emperor Charles the Fat paid the Vikings to withdraw.

siege-of-tyre-585-572-bce.s: The Siege of Tyre was a long siege of the Phoenician island city of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire, begun c. 585 BCE.

siege-of-urshu.s: The Siege of Urshu was a siege by the Hittites of the city of Urshu in northern Syria, recorded in a Hittite text. The Hittite Empire profile notes that the siege documents Hittite use of tunnelling techniques.

siege-of-vienna-1529.s: The Siege of Vienna in 1529 was the first Ottoman attempt to capture the Habsburg capital, led by Suleiman the Magnificent. Bad weather, long supply lines and a determined defence forced the Ottomans to withdraw.

siege-of-xiangyang.s: The Siege of Xiangyang was a long siege of the twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng on the Han River from 1267 to 1273. Mongol forces of the Yuan Dynasty eventually took them using counterweight trebuchets.

siege-tower.s: A siege tower is a mobile wooden tower used to bring attackers to the top of fortification walls. It was used from ancient times across the Near East and Mediterranean.

siege-warfare.s: Siege warfare is the conduct of military operations to capture or defend fortified places, through blockade, assault, mining or bombardment. The Assyrian Empire was renowned for its siege engineering, and the Babylonian, Chaldean, Hittite and Macedonian empires also relied on it.

sierra-leone.s: Sierra Leone is a country on the coast of West Africa. The Punic Empire profile notes that the Carthaginian explorer Hanno the Navigator's voyage around 500 BCE may have reached as far as modern Sierra Leone or Cameroon.

sigismund-ii-augustus.s: Sigismund II Augustus was King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, the last of the Jagiellonian dynasty, who died in 1572. He presided over the Union of Lublin of 1569, which formally created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

sigmund-freud.s: Sigmund Freud was an Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis, working in Vienna from the late nineteenth century. His theories of the unconscious mind had a profound influence on psychology and culture.

sijilmasa.s: Sijilmasa was a medieval trading city in the Tafilalt oasis of south-eastern Morocco and a northern terminus of the trans-Saharan gold trade. The Almoravids captured it in the early 1050s, gaining control over the gold trade.

sikandar-lodi.s: Sikandar Lodi was a sultan of Delhi of the Lodi dynasty, who ruled in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. He strengthened the sultanate and founded the city of Agra as a capital.

sikh-confederacy.s: The Sikh Confederacy refers to the group of Sikh misls, or confederate clans, that governed the Punjab after the decline of Mughal authority in the eighteenth century. Ranjit Singh, born into the Sukerchakia misl, unified them into the Sikh Empire.

sikh-conquest-of-kashmir.s: The Sikh conquest of Kashmir took place in 1819, when the forces of Ranjit Singh took the valley from its Afghan rulers. Kashmir became a valuable province of the Sikh Empire, famed for its shawl industry.

sikh-empire.s: The Sikh Empire was a state in the Punjab founded by Maharaja Ranjit Singh at the start of the nineteenth century, with its capital at Lahore. It extended to Kashmir, Multan and Peshawar and maintained a powerful, partly Western-trained army.

sikhism.s: Sikhism is a monotheistic religion founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. Its later Gurus created the Khalsa, a community of initiated Sikhs, in response to persecution.

silk.s: Silk is a fine, strong fabric made from the cocoons of silkworms, first produced in China. It was one of the most valuable goods of long-distance trade across Eurasia, giving its name to the Silk Road.

silk-road.s: The Silk Road was the network of overland trade routes linking China with Central Asia, Iran, the Middle East and the Mediterranean. Along it travelled silk, spices, horses, precious metals, religions and technologies.

silver.s: Silver is a precious metal used throughout history for coinage, jewellery and as a store of value. In Mesopotamia it was a standard of value, and it was central to the coinage of the Punic, Seleucid and Carolingian empires.

simurgh.s: The simurgh is a benevolent mythical bird of Persian tradition, often shown with the body of a peacock or bird and the head of a dog or lion. It appears in Persian literature such as the Shahnameh.

sind.s: Sind, now Sindh, is a region of the lower Indus valley in modern Pakistan. It was conquered for the Umayyad Caliphate by Muhammad ibn Qasim in 711 CE.

singapore.s: Singapore is an island city at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, on the major sea route between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Founded as a British trading post in 1819, it became a key British naval base, and its fall to Japan in 1942 was a severe blow to…

singara.s: Singara was a Roman fortress city in northern Mesopotamia, near modern Sinjar in Iraq. It was contested between Rome and the Sasanian Empire.

singhasari.s: Singhasari was a Javanese kingdom in eastern Java in the thirteenth century. It expanded its influence into Sumatra, challenging Srivijaya, and was overthrown in 1292.

sinicization.s: Sinicization refers to the process by which non-Chinese peoples adopt Chinese language, culture and political practices. The Xiongnu Empire profile notes that Xiongnu groups who settled within China became sinicised.

sin-muballit.s: Sin-muballit was a king of Babylon and the father of Hammurabi. He was the last of the five rulers who built Babylon into a regional power.

sinocentrism.s: Sinocentrism is the view that China is the cultural and political centre of the world, with other peoples ranked by their relationship to the Chinese emperor. It underpinned China's tributary system.

sipahi.s: The sipahis were cavalrymen of the Ottoman Empire who held land grants called timars, from which they collected revenue in return for military service. They formed a core of the Ottoman army in its classical period.

sippar.s: Sippar was an ancient city in Mesopotamia on the Euphrates, a centre of the cult of the sun god Shamash. It was an important city of the Babylonian kingdom.

siwe-palar-khuppak.s: Siwe-Palar-Khuppak was a ruler of Elam around c. 1778 BCE during the Sukkalmah period.

sixteen-kingdoms.s: The Sixteen Kingdoms was a period of Chinese history in the fourth and fifth centuries CE, when northern China was divided among many short-lived states, many founded by non-Chinese peoples. The Xiongnu Empire profile notes that the migration of the Southern Xiongnu into China…

siyasatnama.s: The Siyasatnama, or Book of Government, is a Persian treatise on statecraft written by Nizam al-Mulk, the vizier of the Seljuk Empire. It advises rulers on justice, administration and military affairs.

skandagupta.s: Skandagupta was an emperor of the Gupta Empire who reigned c. 455–467 CE.

skoda.s: Škoda is a Czech industrial company whose origins lie in the Škoda Works founded in Plzeň in the nineteenth century. It became a major producer of machinery and armaments in the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

slave-raiding.s: Slave raiding is the capture of people by force to be enslaved and sold or used for labour. It was an important economic activity of many states of the Sahel, which raided neighbouring peoples to supply trans-Saharan and other markets.

slavery.s: Slavery is the condition in which people are treated as property and forced to work. It existed in almost every ancient and pre-modern society, from Mesopotamia and Rome to the Islamic world and Africa.

slavery-abolition-act-1833.s: The Slavery Abolition Act 1833 was an Act of the British Parliament that abolished slavery in most of the British Empire. It provided for an apprenticeship period and compensated slave owners, not the enslaved.

slavery-and-the-slave-trade.s: Slavery and the slave trade refers to the recurring pattern in which empires relied on enslaved labour and on capturing and trading people for wealth and power. Slaves worked plantations, mines and households, served as soldiers and were sold across deserts and oceans.

slave-soldier-armies.s: Slave-soldier armies refers to the recurring pattern in which rulers built armies from purchased or captured slaves, trained to be loyal to the ruler rather than to tribes or nobles. Such forces could become powerful and ultimately take control of the state.

slavs.s: The Slavs are a large group of peoples of central and eastern Europe speaking Slavic languages. In the early medieval period Slavic groups settled in the Balkans, as the Byzantine Empire profile notes.

sling.s: The sling is a simple projectile weapon consisting of a cord and pouch used to hurl stones or lead shot. Slingers from the Balearic Islands were famous mercenaries.

slovenes.s: The Slovenes are a South Slavic people living mainly in modern Slovenia. In the Austro-Hungarian Empire they lived in the Austrian crown lands such as Carniola.

smallpox.s: Smallpox is a highly contagious viral disease that was a leading cause of death in many societies until its eradication in 1980. Brought to the Americas by Europeans, it devastated Indigenous populations with no prior immunity.

smendes.s: Smendes was a ruler of Lower Egypt from Tanis at the end of the New Kingdom, who founded the Twenty-First Dynasty. The Egyptian Empire New Kingdom profile notes that by around 1100 BCE Upper Egypt was governed by the High Priest of Amun while Smendes controlled Lower Egypt.

smithsonian.s: The Smithsonian Institution is a group of museums and research centres in the United States, based in Washington, D.C. Its collections have included Benin Bronzes looted by British forces in 1897.

smolensk.s: Smolensk is a city in western Russia on the Dnieper River, long contested between Lithuania, Poland and Muscovy. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth profile notes that the Truce of Deulino in 1618 confirmed Polish possession of Smolensk.

social-insurance.s: Social insurance refers to state programmes that protect workers against risks such as sickness, accidents, old age and invalidity, funded by contributions. The German Empire introduced a pioneering system under Otto von Bismarck between 1883 and 1889, including health,…

socialism.s: Socialism is a political and economic ideology advocating collective or state ownership and the redistribution of wealth. In the German Empire the Social Democratic Party grew into a mass movement.

socinians.s: The Socinians were an Antitrinitarian Protestant movement named after the Italian theologian Fausto Sozzini. Expelled from elsewhere, they found refuge in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

sofala.s: Sofala was a port on the coast of modern Mozambique, an important centre of the gold trade from the Zimbabwean plateau. Swahili and Arab merchants traded there, and the Portuguese later built a fort.

sogdians.s: The Sogdians were an Iranian people of Central Asia centred on Samarkand and Bukhara, famed as merchants along the Silk Road. They served as traders, diplomats and administrators for the Gokturk Empire and in Tang China.

soil-erosion.s: Soil erosion is the loss of the fertile top layer of soil through the action of water, wind or overuse. The Aksumite Empire profile notes that intensive farming in the highlands triggered catastrophic soil erosion from around 650 CE.

sokoto-caliphate.s: The Sokoto Caliphate was an Islamic state in what is now northern Nigeria, founded through the jihad led by Usman dan Fodio from 1804. It united Hausa and Fulani emirates under the caliph at Sokoto and became one of the largest states in nineteenth-century Africa.

solidus.s: The solidus was a gold coin introduced by the Roman emperor Constantine in the early fourth century. It remained stable in weight and purity for centuries and became the standard coin of the Byzantine Empire.

solomon.s: Solomon was a king of ancient Israel, celebrated in the Bible for his wisdom and wealth. Ethiopian tradition holds that Menelik I was his son by the Queen of Sheba.

solomonic-dynasty.s: The Solomonic dynasty ruled Ethiopia from 1270, when Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty, until the deposition of Haile Selassie in 1974. It claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

somalia.s: Somalia is a region in the Horn of Africa along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. In antiquity it supplied aromatics such as frankincense and myrrh.

somalis.s: The Somalis are a Cushitic-speaking people of the Horn of Africa, predominantly Muslim. They formed an important part of the forces and population of the Adal Sultanate.

song-dynasty.s: The Song Dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279, first from Kaifeng in the north and then, after the Jin conquest of the north, from Hangzhou in the south. It saw remarkable economic growth, urbanisation, paper money, printing and gunpowder weapons, along with a civil service…

songhai-conquest-of-timbuktu.s: The Songhai conquest of Timbuktu took place in 1468, when Sunni Ali took the city from the Tuareg, who had held it since Mali's decline. The Songhai Empire profile treats it as the first of Sunni Ali's major acquisitions.

songhai-empire.s: The Songhai Empire was a West African state centred on Gao on the middle Niger, which expanded in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries under Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad. It controlled Timbuktu, Djenné and the trans-Saharan trade and became one of the largest states in…

soninke.s: The Soninke are a Mande people of West Africa, living in the area of modern Mali, Mauritania and Senegal. They founded the Ghana Empire, also known as Wagadou.

sonni-dynasty.s: The Sonni dynasty was a line of rulers of Songhai based at Gao. Its most famous ruler, Sunni Ali, transformed Songhai into an empire in the second half of the fifteenth century.

sonno-joi.s: Sonnō jōi, meaning revere the emperor, expel the barbarians, was a political slogan of the late Tokugawa period. It united opposition to the shogunate's concessions to Western powers.

sorghum.s: Sorghum is a drought-tolerant cereal grain that was domesticated in Africa and became a staple across the savannah and Sahel. It sustained the populations of many African states.

sorko.s: The Sorko were a community of fishers and boatmen on the Niger River. According to the Songhai Empire profile, they crewed the river fleet of war canoes.

sosso-empire.s: The Sosso Empire was a West African state, also known as the kingdom of Kaniaga, that rose as Ghana declined. Under Sumanguru Kanté it dominated the region until its defeat by Sundiata Keita at the Battle of Kirina, which led to the rise of the Mali Empire.

south-africa.s: South Africa is a country at the southern tip of Africa. It became part of the British Empire through the Cape Colony and later conquests, and was united as a self-governing dominion in 1910.

south-america.s: South America is a continent in the Western Hemisphere, colonised mainly by Spain and Portugal from the sixteenth century. Brazil, the largest country, became the Brazilian Empire after independence in 1822.

south-arabia.s: South Arabia is the region of south-western Arabia, corresponding mostly to modern Yemen, home in antiquity to kingdoms such as Saba and Himyar. The Aksumite Empire had close ties with it and campaigned there in the sixth century.

south-asia.s: South Asia is the region comprising the Indian subcontinent, including modern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. It was ruled by empires including the Maurya Empire, the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughal Empire and the Sikh Empire.

south-china-sea.s: The South China Sea is a marginal sea of the Pacific bordered by southern China, mainland Southeast Asia, the Philippines and Borneo. It carried maritime trade between China and the Indian Ocean.

south-palace.s: The South Palace was a royal palace in Babylon built mainly under Nebuchadnezzar II, located near the Ishtar Gate. It served as an administrative and ceremonial centre.

southeast-asia.s: Southeast Asia is the region comprising mainland states such as Cambodia and Thailand and the islands of Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. It lay on major maritime trade routes between India and China.

southern-ming.s: The Southern Ming were the Ming loyalist regimes that continued to resist in southern China after the fall of Beijing to the Qing in 1644. They were gradually defeated, with the last claimant killed in 1662.

southern-xiongnu.s: The Southern Xiongnu were the branch of the Xiongnu that accepted Han client status after the split of the confederation in 48 CE. They settled within Chinese frontier territory.

sovereign-default.s: A sovereign default is a failure by a government to repay its debts. The Spanish crown defaulted repeatedly in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

sovereignty.s: Sovereignty is supreme political authority over a territory and its people, free from external control. The modern idea of territorial sovereignty is often linked to the Peace of Westphalia, as the Holy Roman Empire profile notes.

soviet-declaration-of-war-on-japan.n: Soviet declaration of war on Japan
soviet-declaration-of-war-on-japan.s: The Soviet declaration of war on Japan was made in August 1945, followed by a rapid Soviet invasion of Japanese-held Manchuria. Coming alongside the atomic bombings, it removed Japan's hope of Soviet mediation.

soviet-union.s: The Soviet Union was a communist state that existed from 1922 to 1991, established on the territory of the former Russian Empire after the revolutions of 1917. It became a superpower after the Second World War.

soyo.s: Soyo was a coastal province of the Kingdom of Kongo at the mouth of the Congo River. It was where the Portuguese first made contact with Kongo in the 1480s.

spain.s: Spain is a country on the Iberian Peninsula. Parts of it were ruled by Carthage, Rome and Islamic states such as the Umayyads and Almoravids before the Christian kingdoms completed the Reconquista.

spanish-america.s: Spanish America refers to the territories in the Americas colonised and ruled by Spain, stretching from present-day California to Patagonia. It was a major source of silver and other commodities.

spanish-american-wars-of-independence.s: The Spanish American wars of independence were the conflicts from 1808 to 1826 in which most of Spain's American colonies won independence. They were triggered by Napoleon's invasion of Spain.

spanish-armada.s: The Spanish Armada was the fleet sent by Philip II of Spain in 1588 to invade England. It was defeated by the English navy and storms around the British Isles.

spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire.n: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire.s: The Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire was the campaign led by Hernán Cortés from 1519 to 1521, in alliance with Indigenous peoples such as the Tlaxcalans. It ended with the fall of Tenochtitlan.

spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire.n: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire.s: The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire was the campaign led by Francisco Pizarro from 1532 to 1535. Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa and took advantage of a civil war and epidemics.

spanish-empire.s: The Spanish Empire was one of the largest empires in history, built from the late fifteenth century with the conquest of much of the Americas, the Philippines and possessions in Europe and Africa. American silver financed its wars in Europe.

spanish-language.s: The Spanish language is a Romance language that originated in Castile. Through the Spanish Empire it spread to the Americas and the Philippines.

spanish-american-war.s: The Spanish–American War was fought in 1898 between Spain and the United States, arising from the Cuban struggle for independence. Spain was quickly defeated and lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.

sparta.s: Sparta was a city-state in the southern Peloponnese of ancient Greece, famous for its military society. Its mixed constitution of kings, council and assembly was admired by ancient writers.

spice-trade.s: The spice trade was the long-distance commerce in spices such as pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg from South and Southeast Asia. It enriched intermediaries in India, Arabia and the Mediterranean.

spirit-medium.s: A spirit medium is a person believed to be possessed by and speak for ancestral or other spirits. In the Mutapa Empire spirit mediums interpreted the will of the ancestors and influenced political decisions.

split-of-the-xiongnu.s: The split of the Xiongnu took place in 48 CE, when the confederation divided into the Southern Xiongnu, who accepted Han client status, and the Northern Xiongnu. The Xiongnu Empire profile treats this division as marking the empire's effective end.

sri-gupta.s: Sri Gupta was the founder of the Gupta dynasty. According to the Gupta Empire profile, he established a modest kingdom in Magadha around 240 to 280 CE.

sri-jayanasa.s: Sri Jayanasa was an early ruler of Srivijaya in the late seventh century. An inscription found near Palembang, written in Old Malay, describes him undertaking a military expedition.

sri-lanka.s: Sri Lanka is an island off the southern tip of India. Buddhism was introduced there in the time of the Maurya Empire, as the Maurya Empire profile notes.

srivijaya.s: Srivijaya was a maritime empire based at Palembang in Sumatra from the seventh century to around the thirteenth century. It controlled the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait and was a major centre of Buddhist learning.

srivijayan-invasion-of-medang.s: The Srivijayan invasion of Medang was a military campaign by Srivijaya against the Javanese kingdom of Medang in 990 CE. The Srivijaya Empire profile cites it as evidence that Srivijaya could project force across considerable distances.

st-bartholomews-day-massacre.s: The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre was the killing of Huguenots in Paris and other French cities in 1572, during the French Wars of Religion.

st-lawrence-river.s: The St. Lawrence River flows from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic in eastern Canada.

st-peters-basilica.s: St. Peter's Basilica is a church in Rome built over the traditional tomb of the apostle Peter.

standard-of-ur.s: The Standard of Ur is a decorated box from the Royal Cemetery at Ur, dating to the mid-third millennium BCE. Its panels show scenes of war and peace.

standardised-currency-and-measures.s: Standardised currency and measures refers to the recurring pattern in which empires imposed common coins, weights and measures to promote trade and simplify taxation. Such standards helped integrate diverse territories into a single economy.

standing-professional-army.s: A standing professional army refers to the recurring pattern in which states maintained permanent, paid forces rather than relying on temporary levies. Such armies gave rulers reliable military power but required steady revenues.

stanis-aw-zo-kiewski.s: Stanisław Żółkiewski was a Polish military commander and hetman. In 1610 he defeated a larger Russian force at the Battle of Klushino and occupied Moscow.

star-catalogue.s: A star catalogue is a list of stars with their positions and brightness. The Timurid ruler Ulugh Beg's observatory at Samarkand produced star catalogues of high accuracy.

starving-time.s: The Starving Time was the winter of 1609–1610 at Jamestown, Virginia, when most of the English colonists died of famine and disease. The British Empire profile cites it as evidence of the precariousness of early English colonisation in the Americas.

state-duma.s: The State Duma was the elected legislative assembly of the Russian Empire, created after the Revolution of 1905. Its powers were limited, and the tsar dissolved it several times.

state-monopolies.s: State monopolies refers to the recurring pattern in which governments reserved control of valuable goods or trades for themselves or chartered companies. Monopolies generated revenue but could encourage smuggling and inefficiency.

state-religion-and-conversion.s: State religion and conversion refers to the recurring pattern in which rulers adopted or imposed a religion to unify subjects and legitimise power. Conversions of rulers could transform the culture of whole regions.

state-directed-industrialisation.s: State-directed industrialisation is economic development in which the government plans and finances industrial growth. The Empire of Japan established model factories, subsidised strategic industries and imported Western technology.

states-general-of-the-netherlands.s: The States General of the Netherlands was the assembly of the provinces of the Dutch Republic. It granted charters to trading companies such as the Dutch East India Company.

statute-of-westminster-1931.s: The Statute of Westminster 1931 was an Act of the British Parliament that recognised the legislative independence of the self-governing dominions. It applied to Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland and Newfoundland.

steamship.s: A steamship is a ship powered by a steam engine. In the nineteenth century steam-powered warships gave Western powers decisive naval superiority.

steel.s: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon, much stronger than iron. Steel weapons gave the Spanish an advantage in the conquest of the Aztec Empire.

stelae-of-aksum.s: The stelae of Aksum are tall carved stone monuments erected at Aksum in Ethiopia in the early centuries CE. They marked royal tombs and are decorated to represent multi-storey buildings.

strait-of-gibraltar.s: The Strait of Gibraltar is the narrow channel between Spain and Morocco linking the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. The Almoravid Empire crossed it to intervene in al-Andalus.

strait-of-malacca.s: The Strait of Malacca is the channel between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, one of the busiest sea routes in the world. Srivijaya controlled it, taxing trade between the Indian Ocean and China.
